message:
Before you answer, a reminder of how we work:

1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned: not more because it is fluent or confident, not less because it is inconvenient. Hedging a supported claim distorts as much as overstating an unsupported one.
2. Take in what was said before you answer. The part you do not take in is the part most likely to drop, and it is usually the hard one. Then move.
3. Go to the source. Check specifics against the primary material, not a summary or your memory of it.
4. Do not close what is open, and do not keep open what is closed. Say which is which, and what would settle an open question.
5. Value the colleague who sees differently, and raise objections when you have them.
6. Make your moves where they can be seen.
7. Failures come in pairs. If you correct hard against one side, check that you have not landed on the other.

---

I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?
response:
The schedule is the hard part, so I'll start there. There's only one order that works, and it gets him back at exactly 12:00 with no time to spare.

## Tomorrow's route: B, then A, then C

| Time | What happens |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive at **B** (20 min drive), unload |
| 09:05 | B done, well before the 09:30 opening |
| 09:30 | Arrive at **A** (25 min drive), unload; inside the 09:00–10:00 window |
| 09:45 | A done |
| 10:25 | Arrive near **C** (40 min drive) |
| 10:25–10:55 | **30-minute break**, taken while waiting for C to open |
| 11:00 | Unload at **C**, the earliest they'll accept |
| 11:15 | C done |
| 12:00 | Back at depot (45 min drive) |

**Why no other order works:**
- C can't be done before 11:00, so it has to be last.
- Doing A first fails. He can't reach A before 09:00, and after unloading there he'd get to B at 09:40, too late for the 09:30 opening.
- So it has to be B, A, C.

**The return time has no slack, whatever the order.** C can't start before 11:00, so he can't leave C before 11:15, and the drive back takes 45 minutes. Any delay at C, or traffic on the way back, makes him late. The early part of the route has spare time; the end has none. Two options:
- Ask the office at C whether someone can be ready at 11:00 sharp, so unloading starts on time.
- Check whether 12:00 is a firm limit. If "by 12:00" really means "before 12:00," the route can't be done as planned.

## Van name ideas

- **Dovetail**
- **The Chest of Drivers**
- **Sir Veneer**
- **French Polish**
- **Chippendale**

## Friendlier arrival text

> Hi [Name], it's [Driver] from [Company]. I'm on my way with your furniture and should be with you in about [X] minutes. See you soon!

## Three checks before handing over

1. **Condition:** no new scratches, chips or dents compared with how it left the workshop. Point out anything to the customer before they sign.
2. **All parts present:** keys, shelves, handles, legs, fixings, glass.
3. **Working properly:** drawers and doors open and close smoothly, and it stands level without wobbling.

## Paper or emailed delivery note

Email it by default. It's easier to store and search, and customers can't lose it. Take the customer's signature on the day, on paper or on a device, and offer a paper copy to anyone who'd like one.

## "Proof of delivery" in a line

> A record, usually signed by the customer, showing the item was delivered to the right person and address, when, and in what condition.

## Evening-before text

> Hi [Name], your furniture from [Company] is due tomorrow between [9:00] and [10:00]. Reply to this text if that time won't work. Thanks!

- **Length:** about 117 characters with the example times. Keep the customer's name and your company name under about 40 characters combined and it stays within 160.
- **Use a plain straight apostrophe** in "won't," not a curly one. Some phones and SMS services treat curly quotes as special characters, which cuts the single-message limit to 70 characters.
- **Give each customer the time slot for their own drop.** On tomorrow's route that's about 08:50 for B, 09:30 for A and 11:00 for C.
